entities.name: Frederick IV of Baden
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Frederick IV of Baden, born into the powerful House of Zähringen, served as the Prince-Bishop of Utrecht from 1496 until his resignation in 1517, a period marked by intense political and military strife in the Low Countries. As the third son of Christoph I, Margrave of Baden-Baden, Frederick's appointment was a strategic move by Emperor Maximilian I to strengthen imperial influence in the strategically vital Prince-Bishopric, which bordered the expanding Burgundian territories now under Habsburg control. His episcopacy was thus inextricably linked to the larger geopolitical struggles between the Habsburgs, the Duchy of Gelre under Charles of Egmond, and the often rebellious city of Utrecht itself.

Throughout his tenure, Frederick IV struggled to assert his authority over a diocese embroiled in constant warfare and internal dissent. The citizens of Utrecht frequently resisted his rule, preferring bishops with stronger local ties, and his reliance on imperial and Habsburg support often alienated local factions. He faced continuous military challenges from Charles II, Duke of Gelre, who sought to expand his own domain at Utrecht's expense. Unable to maintain peace or effectively govern his temporal territories, Frederick frequently resided outside Utrecht, delegating much of his administrative and military responsibilities to stadtholders appointed by the Habsburgs, further eroding the bishopric's independence. His reign was characterized by a gradual but inexorable shift of temporal power away from the ecclesiastical authority and towards secular rulers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Frederick IV's resignation as Prince-Bishop of Utrecht in 1517 directly led to the transfer of temporal power to Charles V, fundamentally altering the political landscape of the Low Countries by integrating Utrecht into the nascent Habsburg Netherlands.
